thesis: Round 1 found that a short, sharp RSI(3)<15-and-close<bb_lower(10,2) dislocation in liquid semiconductor names resolved (closed back above ema(5)) in a median of 4 sessions with only 4.2% unresolved after 10 -- forced-flow selling exhausting itself fast, not a genuine repricing. Round 2 tests whether that speed is a semiconductor-specific quirk or a broad property of liquid index/sector baskets, using the same mechanism unchanged, over the same 2021-02-13 to 2026-02-13 window, on 24 candidate broad-index, sector, factor and international ETFs. It survives intact: median resolution across the strongest 12 candidates is still 3-4 sessions, with the same signal (rsi(3)<15, close<bb_lower(10,2)) firing 19-37 times per name -- speed is not a semiconductor property, it is a property of how liquid instruments absorb and clear forced selling, whether the forced seller is a single-stock stop cascade or an index-fund redemption wave. What differs from round 1, as the brief predicted, is amplitude, not speed: median bounce at the first ema(5) reclaim across this universe is roughly 1-2%, well under round 1's semis' 2.7-2.8%, because a basket has no single-company blow-up risk to overreact to and less of the multiple-expansion-and-compression that drives an outsized single-stock air-pocket. The other side of this trade is the same as round 1: index-fund flow and systematic de-risking extending a drawdown 1-3 sessions past where it settles, clearing into thin liquidity at the print, then unwinding as soon as the flow stops. The mechanically important finding is on sizing, not speed: I tested tightening stop_loss_pct/take_profit_pct down to match the smaller ETF bounce (e.g. 0.04/0.03) and it performs worse, not better -- a tight stop converts a dip that would have recovered on the ema(5) rule into a premature stop-out, since the engine evaluates stops off the previous close with next-open fills and cannot distinguish 'still resolving' from 'broken.' Keeping round 1's stop/take-profit (7%/5%) unchanged and letting the ema(5) rule do almost all of the work (in a 363-trade pooled simulation across the chosen 12 names, 331 of 363 exits, 91%, were the rule, only 4 were stops) produces a 69.4% win rate, mean win +1.62%, mean loss -1.82%, realized RRR approx 0.89 -- better than round 1's 0.71, because this universe's typical adverse excursion before resolving is small (median close-to-close drawdown during the hold was near zero to -1% for most names) even though its bounce is smaller too. A single large loss is still what erases this edge, and this universe adds a new version of that risk round 1's single-name semis did not have as acutely: same-day signal clustering. Because these are broad-market and sector proxies, the same broad-selloff day that dislocates SPY also dislocates 8-11 of the other 11 names simultaneously (verified on 2021-09-20, 2022-06-10, 2023-09-21 and five other dates) -- the 0.581 mean pairwise sector correlation this brief measured is exactly why. max_positions=6 at position_pct=0.15 (90% of book) caps how much of that pile-on the strategy can actually take, but it cannot prevent the remaining six positions from moving together if the broad drawdown continues past the median 3-4 session resolution window.
